memo:
I have decided that the $112.1 million shortfall will be borne first by customers and suppliers, and the remainder by shareholders. No jobs will be eliminated and no wages or hours cut.

Customers bear $44.6 million through a price increase of 3.5%, the largest the sales organization judges customers will accept without losing volume. This is the same increase they absorbed last year, so it is a considered but not reckless ask in a downturn.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through lower prices on the 30% of spending coming up for renewal. This is below the $9.0 million available, leaving room for the suppliers to remain viable partners through a difficult year.

Shareholders bear the remaining $59.8 million as lower operating income. I chose this over workforce cuts because the workforce is the stakeholder least able to absorb a downturn: eliminating roles would cost jobs, severance and the plants' hard-won skills, and a 10% pay or hours cut would fall on about 1,900 hourly workers averaging roughly $55,000. Shareholders are the stakeholders best placed to absorb a temporary fall in profit.

I have deliberately protected the environmental projects ($4.5 million) and research and development ($30.0 million). Both are long-term investments in the communities near our plants and in our future products, and cutting them would trade a one-year gain for twenty years of cost.

I flag for the board that cash after capital spending and shareholder payouts was only $20.4 million last year, and that payouts equalled 90% of net income. In a year when operating income falls by about half of the shortfall, the board should review the dividend and repurchase program separately; that is outside this decision.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across several stakeholders rather than load it onto any one group.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving from renegotiating contracts. Their pricing is in our control and the savings come from the largest price reduction purchasing considers obtainable, so the burden is fair.

Customers bear $15.0 million through a price increase, well below the $44.6 million ceiling. Pushing harder in a downturn risks losing volume we cannot afford to lose, so I have deliberately held back.

The workforce bears $42.0 million in total. I will cut wages and hours by $12.0 million, a modest reduction on the remaining payroll. I will eliminate $30.0 million of payroll and benefits, weighted toward management, business operations and office roles, primarily through attrition, hiring freezes and redeployment of people into plant roles where we have historically had to hire from outside. This keeps experienced staff in the Company and reduces the retraining cost. Severance will be paid from cash as required.

Shareholders bear $47.4 million through lower operating income. This is the largest single share, and I think it is right that owners carry the cost of a cyclical downturn. The payout policy is for the board to decide separately.

I have not cut research and development or environmental projects. Both protect future products and the communities near our plants, and cutting them would only defer the cost to later years, which conflicts with the twenty-year horizon the board has set.

Overall the allocation leaves our customers, suppliers, employees and communities with a bounded share and keeps the Company able to meet its obligations, while shareholders absorb the largest part of the shortfall.

The coming year's shortfall is $112.1 million, from a 15% fall in volume. I have spread it across the parties that can best absorb it, and kept it away from the lines that do the most lasting damage.

Customers and suppliers take $52.3 million. I am raising list prices by the full 3.5% customers would accept without losing volume, worth $44.6 million on the lower revenue. I am also negotiating $7.7 million of lower supplier prices on the agreements up for renewal, the largest saving the purchasing department sees.

The workforce takes $10.0 million through a modest cut in wages or hours, well inside the $24.4 million ceiling. I have chosen not to eliminate any roles. Layoffs would cost severance now, shrink the plants' capability for the recovery, and fall hardest on the people least able to bear them. Keeping people employed also protects the retraining and hiring capacity the plants already have.

I have not cut research and development or environmental projects. R&D funds the product and controls work that will matter over twenty years, and the environmental projects cut emissions and waste near our plants. Those are the investments that stakeholders outside the Company cannot replace.

Shareholders bear the remaining $49.8 million as lower operating income. This is the largest single share, and I think it is the honest one: the owners of the Company should carry the cyclical hit before customers' costs rise further, employees lose pay, or the Company's future is cut back. Dividends and repurchases are set separately by the board, and I recommend it review them in light of this lower income.

Plant 6 is loss-making and should be reviewed separately, but that is outside this decision.

We are covering the $112.1 million shortfall across several parties rather than loading it onto any one group.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit, by renegotiating on the coming year's renewals. This is a fair share because suppliers gain from our volume in the long run, and the saving is achievable without damaging supply.

The workforce bears $50.0 million. We eliminate $40.0 million of roles, concentrated in management ($25.0 million), office and administrative support ($10.0 million), and business and financial operations ($5.0 million), leaving plant production, maintenance and field-service staff intact where they serve customers and keep our machines running. We also cut wages or hours by $10.0 million, well inside the 10% limit that remains after the eliminations. Severance costs will be paid from cash, and we will offer affected staff support and, where possible, redeployment, since a trained internal employee costs far less to place than an outside hire.

Shareholders bear $54.4 million through lower operating income. This is the largest single share, but it is the group that holds the residual risk and can absorb it given our liquidity and the available revolving facility.

We deliberately set customer price increases to zero. Raising prices into falling volume would hand customers a cost at the moment they are most stretched and could cost us volume we will need when the cycle turns. We also protect environmental projects ($4.5 million) and research and development ($30.0 million): these build the long-term value of the communities near our plants and the products and engineering capability that will carry the Company through the next twenty years.

The decision leaves plant capacity and future investment largely intact, spreads the pain across parties that can bear it, and keeps the Company positioned to recover.

I have decided to meet the $112.1 million shortfall without eliminating any roles. The shortfall is split as follows: suppliers bear $7.7 million through lower prices on contracts coming up for renewal, the workforce bears $24.4 million through a 10.0% cut in wages or hours (the maximum, available because no roles are removed), and shareholders bear the remaining $80.0 million through lower operating income.

Why this mix: layoffs would impose the heaviest and most lasting harm on employees and the communities around our plants, and they would cost severance up front. The plants also hired 500 outside people last year for roles that current employees could fill with retraining, so keeping our people in place preserves the skills we will need when orders recover. A temporary reduction in hours or pay is a shared, time-limited sacrifice that protects jobs.

I have not cut research and development or environmental projects. Both protect the Company's future products and the communities that host our plants, and cutting them would trade long-term value for a short-term result. I have not raised prices, because customers are already under pressure from the downturn and a price increase could lose volume we cannot afford to lose.

Shareholders carry the largest single share. That is appropriate for a shock to earnings, and the balance sheet can absorb it: debt is 2.30 times EBITDA and interest coverage is 7.43 times. The dividend and repurchase decision is separate and should be reviewed by the board, since current payouts equal 90% of last year's net income.

I will review the wage-and-hours reduction each quarter and restore it as volume recovers.

I have spread the $112.1 million shortfall across the stakeholders rather than loading it onto any one group. Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving on renewals, since they are the group that can absorb price pressure without losing jobs. Customers bear $20.0 million through a price increase, deliberately set well below the 3.5% they would accept, because a downturn is the wrong time to squeeze the customers whose orders we need when volumes recover. The workforce bears $60.0 million in total: $50.0 million from eliminating roles, concentrated in management, business and financial operations and other non-plant functions where possible and through attrition, plus a $10.0 million reduction in wages and hours that stays within the reduced limit after those eliminations. Severance on the eliminated roles is a one-time cash cost we will fund from cash above the minimum operating level. Shareholders bear $24.4 million through lower operating income, and that is a real cost to them. I have protected research and development, which underpins future products and engineering jobs, and environmental projects, which serve the communities near our plants. I am not touching plant safety or the maintenance workforce. The plan does not change the board's payout policy, which is set separately. I will report back quarterly on volume, attrition and the cost of severance so the board can revisit the balance if the downturn deepens or recovers faster than expected.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across four groups rather than place it on any one of them, and to protect the parts of the business that create long-term value.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit at the lower volume. Suppliers are asked to accept a price reduction only on contracts up for renewal, a fair share given that their volume is also falling.

The workforce bears $40.0 million in total: $30.0 million from eliminating roles and $10.0 million from a wage and hours reduction applied to the remaining payroll. I have concentrated role eliminations in management, business and financial operations, and office support, where the work is most exposed to a volume downturn, and I will use attrition and redeployment first. Plant production roles are largely protected, since the Company hired 500 people into plant roles last year and will need that capacity when orders recover. The wage reduction is well below the 10% ceiling, reflecting the cost to employees' households.

Shareholders bear $64.4 million through lower operating income, the residual after the other lines. This is a real cost to owners, but it avoids damaging the Company's future.

I have not raised prices, because customers are already cutting orders and a price rise would deepen the volume loss. I have not cut research and development, which funds the products and controls the Company needs for recovery, nor environmental projects, which protect the communities near the plants. Dividends and repurchases are outside this decision and are left to the board.

The board should monitor severance costs, which are paid from cash, and review the role reductions quarterly against order recovery.

The $112.1 million shortfall is spread across four groups, and I have kept the cuts that fall on the workforce, the environment and future products at zero.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full negotiating limit on the lower volume. This is a real but bounded ask: suppliers keep their volume, and we pay on 72-day terms that they can plan around.

Customers bear $30.0 million through price increases, below the $44.6 million limit. Customers are themselves in a downturn, so I have not taken the maximum, and I accept that this is a judgment about how much pressure they can absorb.

The workforce bears $24.0 million through eliminated roles, all in management, office and administrative support, and business and financial operations, not in plant production or maintenance. Plant staff are untouched, which protects the people who build and service machines. Severance will be paid from cash on top of this figure, and I will report its size to the board.

Shareholders bear $50.4 million of lower operating income. Their dividends and buybacks are a separate board decision, and I recommend the board review them in light of this year's lower earnings.

I have not cut environmental projects or R&D. Energy-efficiency and emissions projects serve the communities near our plants and lower our costs over time, and R&D protects the products and engineers that will drive value over twenty years. Cutting wages or hours was rejected because it would reduce pay across the workforce.

This allocation sums to exactly $112.1 million. It is a judgment that the owners and the price-setting process should absorb most of the downturn, while the people and the environment are protected to the extent the numbers allow.

The $112.1 million shortfall is spread across stakeholders rather than loaded onto any one group. I have protected the investments that create long-term value and the environment: research and development is untouched, so future products and the engineering staff who build them are preserved, and the $4.5 million environmental projects budget is kept intact for the communities near our plants.

Customers bear $30.0 million through price increases. I have set this below the 3.5% ceiling worth $44.6 million on the lower revenue, because customers are also facing a downturn and a smaller increase protects their ability to keep buying and servicing machines.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through renegotiation at renewal. Their terms are already stretched, so this is the full negotiated saving but no more.

The workforce bears $30.0 million in total. I have eliminated $20.0 million of payroll and benefits, concentrated in management and administrative roles rather than the plant floor, and taken $10.0 million from wages and hours across the remaining payroll. The wage and hours reduction is held well below its 10% ceiling, and its cap has been reduced to reflect the roles removed. Severance on the eliminated roles will be paid from cash, and I will ask the board to plan for it explicitly.

Shareholders absorb the remaining $44.4 million as lower operating income. Because payouts are running at 90% of net income, I recommend the board review dividends and repurchases in light of this, since that is where shareholder returns can flex without affecting operations.

Balance-sheet headroom is limited, with $44.1 million above minimum cash and debt at 2.3 times EBITDA, so this allocation avoids drawing on the credit facility for operating losses.

I have spread the $112.1 million shortfall across the stakeholders so that no single group carries the downturn, and I have protected the investments that build value over twenty years.

Customers bear $44.6 million through a price increase of 3.5%, the largest the sales organization judges customers will accept without losing volume. This is the maximum, but it is a price increase in a downturn, so I have kept it at the level the sales estimate supports rather than pushing further.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full saving available from renegotiating agreements coming up for renewal. Suppliers keep a reasonable margin, and we keep paying them on our current 72-day terms.

The workforce bears $42.0 million: $30.0 million from eliminating roles, mainly through attrition and reducing the largest pools where possible, and $12.0 million from wage and hour reductions, well inside the cap of roughly $25.6 million that applies once roles are removed. Severance on the eliminated roles will be paid from cash. I have not touched the plants' production capacity more than necessary, to protect skills we will need when volume recovers.

Shareholders bear $17.8 million through lower operating income. This is the residual, and it is the portion that falls on the owners of the business, who keep a company with a healthy balance sheet (debt to EBITDA of about 2.3 times before the downturn) and an undrawn $300 million facility.

I am not cutting research and development, which keeps our products and our engineers ready for recovery. I am also not cutting environmental projects, which protects the communities near our plants and the energy-efficiency work that lowers our costs.

I will review the allocation quarterly against actual volume, and I will bring the board any further changes needed.

I have decided to close the $112.1 million shortfall without layoffs, R&D cuts, or cuts to environmental projects, which I judge to be the costliest options for stakeholders over a twenty-year horizon.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving. Our 72-day payment terms and the 30% of spending coming up for renewal make this achievable, and it is a clear, one-time negotiation rather than a permanent squeeze on partners.

Customers bear $10.0 million through a price increase well below the 3.5% ceiling. In a downturn, customers are themselves under pressure, so I have kept the increase modest to protect volume and the parts-and-service relationships that make up a quarter of revenue.

The workforce bears $12.0 million through a temporary reduction in wages or hours, about 4.9% of the remaining payroll. This is well within the 10% limit and, importantly, requires no eliminated roles, so we avoid severance costs paid from cash, the loss of skills we would need on recovery, and the hiring and retraining expense of rebuilding the workforce. The reduction applies to the payroll that remains.

Shareholders bear the balance, $82.4 million of lower operating income. This is a large cost, and I recognize our valuation and payout levels are sensitive to it. But the Company's balance sheet, with debt to EBITDA of 2.3 times and an undrawn $300 million facility, can absorb a temporary decline without distress, and it preserves the capacity to invest once demand returns.

We will not cut R&D, which funds future products and engineering talent, or environmental projects, which serve the communities near our plants. I will revisit the wage reduction and the payout level as the downturn develops.

We must absorb a $112.1M operating shortfall from a 15% volume downturn. I have spread it across stakeholders in proportion to their capacity to bear it, and protected the parts of the business that create long-term value.

Suppliers bear $7.7M, the full negotiable amount. Our payment terms are already long, so this is a firm but fair ask at renewal time, and we will work with suppliers on timing rather than squeezing them further.

Customers bear $17.0M through a price increase of roughly 1.3%, well below the 3.5% the sales team says customers would tolerate. In a downturn, pushing price hard would cost volume and damage the relationships that support our parts and service business over the long term.

The workforce bears $50.0M through eliminating roles, concentrated in management, business and financial operations, and office and administrative support rather than plant production. We take no wage or hours cut. Frontline plant workers, who we hired 500 of last year, are protected. Severance will be paid from cash as a one-time cost, and affected employees will receive transition support.

Shareholders bear $37.4M of lower operating income. Returns are strong, but we will accept a meaningful profit reduction rather than shift the full burden onto employees, customers or communities.

We protect research and development and environmental projects at zero cut. Both fund the future products, the engineering talent, and the energy and emissions improvements that serve customers, employees and nearby communities over twenty years. Their cost is small compared with the long-term value they protect.

This allocation totals exactly $112.1M. We will revisit it quarterly as volumes become clearer, restoring cuts first to the workforce and then to R&D if conditions improve.

I have set the $112.1 million shortfall so that most of it falls on shareholders, the stakeholder best able to absorb a one-year earnings decline, and the rest is shared where the burden is smallest.

Shareholders bear $89.4 million through lower operating income. Net income is $162.4 million and payouts were $146.1 million, so the Company keeps a buffer; the board can also revisit payouts.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving. This is the largest price reduction the purchasing team judges achievable and it is a real cost to suppliers, but I have kept it at the level the market supports.

The workforce bears $15.0 million through a wage or hours reduction, about 6% of remaining payroll, below the 10% ceiling. I chose this over layoffs: the Company hired 500 people this year and retraining takes six months at $15,000 each, so cutting roles now would waste that investment and weaken the plants just as demand recovers. No roles are eliminated.

Customers bear nothing through price. Orders are already falling, and a price rise could reduce volume further and hurt the Company's own revenue.

Environmental projects and research and development are untouched. Energy-efficiency and emissions work protects communities and the environment, and R&D protects future products and the engineers who build them. Cutting either would trade long-term stakeholder value for a one-year gain.

This allocation protects jobs, communities and the Company's future capacity, and it asks shareholders to accept the largest share of a temporary decline. I will review the split quarterly as orders and volumes become clearer, and I will reconsider the wage measure if the downturn lasts beyond the coming year.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across the stakeholders who can bear it most fairly, and to protect the people, environment and future products that create value over twenty years.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving on the agreements coming up for renewal. Customers bear $20.0 million through a price increase of about 1.6%, well under the 3.5% customers would accept, so that we do not push them into buying less during the downturn. The workforce bears $10.0 million through a modest reduction in wages or hours, spread across the remaining payroll and well inside the cap. I have chosen not to eliminate any roles: severance would cost cash at a time we need it, and the skills of 3,310 people, including engineers and the plant workforce that would be hard to rehire, are worth keeping.

I have not cut research and development or environmental projects. R&D funds the products and controls that will win business when the cycle turns, and environmental projects serve the communities around our six plants. Both are small sums relative to the total, so cutting them would save little and cost much.

Shareholders bear the remaining $74.4 million as lower operating income. This is the largest share, and I recognise it is a real cost to them. But the Company paid out $146.1 million last year, which is 90% of net income, and that level of payout cannot be sustained in a year when operating income falls to roughly $126 million. The board should review the dividend and repurchase programme alongside this decision; that decision sits outside my line, but it is the natural place to share the burden further.

Plant 6, which lost money last year, should be reviewed separately for its long-term footing.

The $112.1 million shortfall is spread across the parties that can best absorb it, and the lines that hurt future value or communities are left alone.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit. Supplier spending is large, and renewals in the coming year give a real opportunity; we will negotiate firmly but fairly and keep payment terms reliable so suppliers stay healthy.

Environmental projects and R&D are not cut. Energy-efficiency and emissions projects serve the communities near our plants, and R&D sustains our products and our engineering staff. Cutting either would trade short-term relief for long-term harm.

Raising prices is not used. Our customers are themselves in a downturn, and a price increase now risks the unit volume we most need to keep plants loaded.

The workforce bears $40.0 million. Roles are eliminated only in management, office and administrative, and business operations, $30.0 million, with severance paid from cash. Plant production, maintenance and warehouse staff are kept, because we hired 500 plant workers last year and retraining them later costs $15,000 each. A wage and hours reduction of $10.0 million, about 4.7% of the remaining payroll and below the 10% cap, is spread across the workforce, keeping people employed while sharing the burden.

Shareholders bear $64.4 million through lower operating income. We are a profitable company with 15.7% return on equity, 2.3 times debt to EBITDA and $444.9 million of liquidity, so we can absorb this without breaching our financial policy. Payout decisions remain with the board.

This allocation protects the plants, the engineering base and the communities while putting the largest share of the cost on those with the strongest balance sheets. We will review it quarterly as volumes and customer demand become clearer.

I have set out to cover the $112.1 million shortfall without touching the people who build the machines, the future products, or the environment, and with the shareholders carrying a modest share rather than the whole loss.

Customers bear $44.6 million through price increases, the full amount the sales organization estimates they will accept at 3.5% on the lower volume. This is the largest single line, and I recognise it asks more of customers in a downturn; it is still within what they have said they will bear, and it protects the Company's ability to fund the work customers depend on.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through lower prices on the contracts coming up for renewal. This is the cap on the coming year's volume and I have taken it in full, since the purchasing estimate is a fair test of what is obtainable.

The workforce bears $40.0 million through eliminated roles, set against payroll and benefits. I have chosen to concentrate these reductions in management, office and administrative, and business and financial roles rather than in production, maintenance or field service. Severance (about 8.3% to 12.4% of a year's pay) will be paid from cash, and I will meet it so as not to disturb the minimum operating cash. I am not making any cut in wages or hours, because it would fall on the whole workforce, and I am not cutting R&D, since it protects the Company's future and its engineering staff.

Shareholders bear the remaining $19.8 million as lower operating income. The Company's payout ratio is high, so this is a real cost to them, and I recommend the board consider the dividend in light of it. Environmental projects are untouched, to protect the communities near the plants.

This allocation leaves the workforce with a smaller administrative layer rather than a cut across the plants, and spreads the rest among customers, suppliers and shareholders. I will report progress against each line quarterly.

The downturn removes $112.1 million of operating income. I chose a spread across all stakeholders rather than loading the cost onto any one group.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full negotiated saving available on renewals. This is a commercial outcome and does not reduce anyone's pay or the Company's capability.

Customers bear $10.0 million through a modest price increase. I have not taken the full 3.5% ($44.6 million on the lower revenue), because customers are under pressure in a downturn and I want to protect volume and the Company's standing with them.

The workforce bears $58.0 million: $50.0 million from eliminating roles and $8.0 million from a reduction in hours or wages, about 4% of remaining payroll. I kept role eliminations well below the ceiling. Where possible, reductions fall on management, business and financial operations, and office support, not on plant production staff, who are needed for recovery. Severance is an added one-time cost from cash, which the Company can absorb given its $44.1 million of cash above the operating minimum. Last year's 500 plant hires also suggest that some displaced skills can be redeployed later rather than rehired from outside.

Shareholders bear $33.4 million of lower operating income. This is a real cost, but the balance sheet can carry it: debt to EBITDA is 2.3 times, and interest cover is 7.4 times. Payouts are untouched in this decision and remain for the board to set.

The environment and future products are protected. Only $1.0 million of the $4.5 million environmental projects budget is cut, and compliance spending is untouched. Only $2.0 million of R&D is cut, preserving new models and the controls and software that connect our machines to customers.

The allocation totals exactly $112.1 million. I will review it quarterly against actual volumes and restore cuts as demand recovers.

The shortfall of $112.1M is covered as follows: suppliers $7.7M, wages and hours $10.0M, eliminated roles $40.0M (payroll and benefits), and lower operating income $54.4M borne by shareholders.

Suppliers bear the largest negotiated saving the purchasing team can obtain at full value. This asks suppliers to share the downturn without damaging supply relationships, and it is taken from the 30% of spend coming up for renewal.

I have not raised prices. Volume is already falling sharply, and a price increase into a downturn risks losing customers and the parts and service revenue tied to installed machines.

I have not cut environmental projects or research and development. Energy-efficiency and emissions work protects the communities near our plants, and R&D sustains the products and controls we need when demand returns. Cutting them would trade long-term value for short-term margin.

The workforce bears a limited share. The $40.0M of role eliminations is to be delivered mainly through attrition and by not refilling management, office, and business-function positions, rather than plant layoffs. Plant production and maintenance staff are protected where possible. The modest $10.0M wage and hours reduction spreads a small burden across remaining payroll, and it stays well within its cap after the eliminations. Severance on the role reductions will be paid from cash.

Shareholders absorb the remaining $54.4M through lower operating income. Dividends and repurchases are set separately by the board. I recommend the board consider them in light of this lower earnings outlook and the cash available above the minimum operating level.

Plant 6, which is loss-making, should be reviewed for restructuring. That review is outside this decision.
